Facebook's new front-end server design delivers on performance without sucking up power - Engineering at Meta (https://engineering.fb.com/2016/03/09/data-center-engineering/facebook-s-new-front-end-server-design-delivers-on-performance-without-sucking-up-power/)
citeturn16view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://engineering.fb.com/2016/03/09/data-center-engineering/facebook-s-new-front-end-server-design-delivers-on-performance-without-sucking-up-power/","lineno":null}); Total lines: 148
L0: POSTED ON MARCH 9, 2016 TO cite0†Data Center Engineering L1: #
L2: 
L3: Facebook’s new front-end server design delivers on performance without sucking up power
L4: 
L5: cite1†Image: 12679481_984009241689785_465961453_n L6:   * One of the primary goals of efficient data center infrastructure is to extract the maximum amount of compute capacity while expending the least power.
L7:   * At Facebook, our web servers must process an increasingly large number of requests simultaneously while responding to each individual request as quickly as possible. To keep up with this growing performance demand, we have used processors with progressively more power over the past 10 years.
L8:   * Given a finite power capacity, this trend was no longer scalable, and we needed a different solution. So we redesigned our web servers to pack more than twice the compute capacity in each rack while maintaining our rack power budget. We also worked closely with Intel on a new processor to be built into this design.
L9:   * This design provides a significant improvement in performance per watt over the previous generation-over-generation trajectory. With this system implemented, we can achieve the same performance per watt today that would have otherwise required multiple new server generations.
L10: Scaling Facebook’s computing infrastructure to be as efficient and cost-effective as possible has been a consistent focus of our engineering efforts. Over the past several years, we have reimagined nearly every component of our data centers — from custom-designed servers and racks to the software that runs on top of them — and we’ve made our designs open to others in the industry through the Open Compute Project.
L11: One thing that has remained constant in our data centers is the use of two-processor servers with progressively more powerful Intel CPUs. About every two years, Intel provided a new generation of more powerful chips that came with a steady rate of improvement in performance over the previous generation.
L12: But the thirst for higher performance across the industry pushed Intel’s CPUs to operate at an increasing power limit, which became a more difficult problem with every generation and ultimately would stop being scalable.
L13: Rather than leave this problem solely in Intel’s hands and accept the fact that our performance improvement trajectory would flatten over time, we approached Intel about working together to come up with a solution. We worked closely with them on the design of a new processor, and in parallel redesigned our server infrastructure to create a system that would meet our needs and be widely adoptable by the rest of the industry.
L14: The result was a one-processor server with lower-power CPUs, which worked better than the two-processor server for our web workload and is better suited overall to data center workloads. With this new system, not only were we able to avoid the flattening performance trajectory, but we could leapfrog the performance cadence we had been on for the past five server generations, as well. The system also operates within the same rack power budget, making our data centers more efficient than ever before.
L15: ## Defining the problem: Increasing web-server workload
L16: In Facebook’s cluster architecture, each cluster consists of more than 10,000 servers. Most of our user traffic comes through the front-end clusters, and web servers represent a major portion of the front-end cluster. These web servers run HHVM, an open-source virtual machine designed for executing programs written in Hack and PHP. HHVM uses a just-in-time compilation approach to achieve superior performance while maintaining the development flexibility that PHP provides.
L17: At a high level, this workload is simultaneously latency-sensitive and throughput-bound. Each web server needs to respond to a given user request quickly as well as serve requests from multiple users in parallel. In CPU terms, we require good single-thread performance and excellent throughput with a large number of concurrent threads. We have architected this workload so that we can parallelize the requests using PHP’s stateless execution model.
L18: There isn’t much interaction between requests on a given web server, allowing us to efficiently scale out across a large number of machines.
L19: However, because we have a large code base and because each request accesses a large amount of data, the workload tends to be memory-bandwidth-bound and not memory-capacity-bound. The code footprint is large enough that we see pressure on the front end of the CPU (fetching and decoding instructions). This necessitates careful attention to the design of the caches in the processor.
L20: Frequent instruction misses in the l-cache result in front-end stalls, which affect latency and instructions executed per second.
L21: We have been using traditional two-socket servers for more than five server generations now at Facebook. Because our web servers are heavily compute-bound and don’t require much memory capacity, the two-socket servers we had in production had several limitations. The server has a QPI link that connects the processors, which created a NUMA problem. It also requires an accompanying chipset that required more power. We kept pushing the performance (and hence power) envelope.
L22: Intel provided us with 95W, then 115W, and now 120W-130W CPUs to hit our performance targets. Given an 11kW rack level power budget, pushing the limits of CPU power was not scalable, and we were not seeing performance keep up with increased power.
L23: Our current Haswell CPUs are produced based on Intel’s 14 nm process, with the next process generation being 10 nm. Over a number of decades, Intel’s performance improvements have steadily kept in line with Moore’s Law — but more recently their “tick-tock” cycle encompassing a new architecture and process transition has slowed.
L24: Making a server-class CPU is difficult and something that we take for granted. Process transitions are also challenging, especially at such minuscule dimensions. We knew that Intel was solving a hard problem, but since our software was evolving at a rapid pace in parallel, we wanted to take this problem on as well and look at our system design through a new lens.
L25: ## Building windmills, not walls
L26: 
L27: “When the winds of change blow, some people build walls and others choose to build windmills.” —Chinese proverb
L28: Since web servers represent a major portion of the front-end cluster, we decided to focus our optimization efforts on this component of our fleet. Three years ago we started working with Intel to define the details of a new processor called Broadwell-D, part of Intel’s Xeon line of processors, that was better suited to data center workloads rather than enterprise. We minimized the CPU to exactly what we required.
L29: We took out the QPI links, which reduced costs for Intel and removed the NUMA problem for us, given that all servers would be one-socket-based. We designed for it to be a system-on-a-chip (SOC), which integrates the chipset, thus creating a simpler design. This single-socket CPU also has a lower thermal design power (TDP).
L30: At the same time, we redesigned our server infrastructure to accommodate double the number of CPUs per rack within the same power infrastructure. Together, we designed a 4 CPU/sled server and 65W CPU that would land squarely in the sweet spot from a performance and power perspective. Facebook is limited by an 11kW rack power budget. We have 30 servers in a rack. At 120W per CPU, this allowed for 60 CPUs, while 65W would allow for 120 CPUs per rack within the same power infrastructure.
L31: While the math might look straightforward, it required a significant redesign of Intel’s roadmap to develop this new part.
L32: cite2†Image L33: 
L34: Modifying their roadmap is not an easy process given the complexity behind designing and manufacturing a processor. Intel calls this new line of products the Xeon-D line, and has made this line of parts plan of record for broader market adoption. We use Xeon-D and Broadwell-D (BW-D) interchangeably here.
L35: ## Mono Lake
L36: We wanted to build an infrastructure that consisted of a number of simple, modular building blocks, which would allow us to incorporate other compute logic (FPGAs or GPUs) in the future. Mono Lake is the server embodiment of Xeon-D and the building block for our SOC-based server designs. It is a highly simplified board that allows for the SOC to be placed with its associated memory and storage for boot and log. It currently has 32GB RAM and 128GB of storage (boot and log) associated with one Xeon-D CPU.
L37: Future designs can have increased memory and storage if required.
L38: cite3†Image L39: ## Yosemite
L40: 
L41: Process migrations and memory allocations hamper system performance. This becomes increasingly difficult and inefficient as servers send out requests for data to downstream services. After years of trying to fix this in software, we decided to fix it in the hardware and simplify the design in the process.
L42: Yosemite is the sled that incorporates four Mono Lake boards and the associated NIC, where the CPUs are connected to the NIC via PCIe lanes and each server has an independent IP address. This design required the use of a multi-host NIC to aggregate the bandwidth from the four servers. The output of the NIC is currently designed to be 2×25 Gbps, which is dynamically shared across the four CPUs. Aggregating ports at the sled level makes for more efficient usage of the top-of-rack (TOR) ports.
L43: Given that there is no direct link between the servers, the NUMA issue is eliminated by design. CPUs on a given sled can communicate with each other via a simple switch in the NIC rather than going through the TOR switch.
L44: 
L45: cite4†Image cite5†Image cite6†Image L46: ## Performance summary
L47: Xeon-D provides a significant improvement in performance per watt. It allows us to break away from the trajectory we have been on and shows the benefit of working in the sweet spot rather than just pushing the boundaries of single-CPU power performance. The performance of a single 65W processor is reduced compared with a 120W processor, but not significantly, given that the CPU is working at an efficient point in the process.
L48: The gains from doubling the number of CPUs in the rack far outweighed the performance loss of a single processor. Dropping the TDP below 65W dropped the performance per CPU to unacceptable levels. This is one of the reasons why Atom-class processors have not gained a foothold in large-scale distributed workloads.
L49: cite7†Image L50: 
L51: We found that for our web workload, a one-processor system has better performance per watt than a two-processor server. This resulted in a significant performance improvement and got us off the flattening generation-over-generation performance improvement trajectory that we have been on for the past five server generations.
L52: A significant limitation of the current Xeon-D processor is the limited number of memory channels. It currently has two memory channels, which is acceptable for our current generation of web servers. Future SOCs would need to alleviate the memory capacity and bandwidth issues by increasing the number of channels.
L53: LLC cache partitioning is a feature that we have worked closely on with Intel. Given our code size, we plan to create appropriate partitions for hot instructions and frequently accessed data, thus relieving memory bandwidth while improving performance. This is still being implemented in our infrastructure, and we are very excited about the potential benefits of this feature.
L54: All of this was possible due to the close collaboration and tireless work of engineers at Facebook and our industry partners, but our journey is only 1 percent done. Exciting times are ahead!

Meta Muse Specs: What Meta’s Free AI Agent Runs On (https://www.starkinsider.com/2026/09/meta-muse-specs-what-it-runs-on.html)
citeturn17view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://www.starkinsider.com/2026/09/meta-muse-specs-what-it-runs-on.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 150
L0:   * cite0†Culture L1:   * cite1†Filmmaking/Tech L2:   * cite2†Atelier Stark Films†atelierstark.com L3: 
L4: [Input: Search articles...]
L5: 
L6: cite3†News cite1†Tech L7: # Meta Muse: The $0 AI Agent Running on a $40 Server
L8: 
L9: 2 vCPUs, 7.7GB of RAM, no GPU. I asked my Meta AI agent what it runs on. The free tier, weekly quota and all, turns out to be running on hardware you would pay $40 a month to rent.
L10: 
L11: BY cite4†Clinton Stark — 09.22.2026
L12: 
L13: * * *
L14: cite5†Image: The Meta Muse agent profile panel on screen, showing the Musey avatar, a Connected status and personality settings Musey's profile panel. The avatar is the friendly part; the VIBE card underneath is where the personality gets configured.
L15: 
L16: No question, these are interesting times.
L17: One of the first things I wanted to know when I signed up for a cite6†Meta Muse†ai.meta.com agent was the kind of box it ran on. Given that cite7†OpenClaw†openclaw.ai is the talk of 2026, I wondered cite8†how Meta created its own commercial variant , and what was underneath the hood.
L18: 
L19: So, I asked my newly created (and super cute) Muse agent, “Musey,” about itself. Surprisingly, it was quite open and more than willing to provide all the specs and details on its hardware — virtual or otherwise.
L20: ## First, the box
L21: 
L22: Let’s start with the server… or the computer as Muse calls it.
L23: ### Musey's spec sheet, measured live on September 20, 2026
L24: CPU: 2 vCPUs, carved off an AMD EPYC 9D25, which identifies itself as a 126-core, 252-thread part
L25: RAM: 7.7 GB total, roughly 3 GB in use, no swap configured
L26: GPU: None. nvidia-smi is not even installed
L27: Home volume: 100 GB, 1.7 GB used, 98 GB free. Workspace itself is 411 MB
L28: Root filesystem: a separate 7.5 GB overlay, nearly empty
L29: Disk speed: about 177 MB/s sequential write, 644 MB/s sequential read (direct I/O)
L30: Media type: reports as non-rotational, so SSD-backed
L31: OS: Ubuntu, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, x86_64
L32: Uptime at time of asking: about 90 minutes, load average 0.19
L33: These are one agent’s measurements of its own machine. Meta publishes none of it, none of it is a commitment, and your account may differ.
L34: 
L35: cite9†Image: Meta Muse agent spec sheet listing 2 vCPUs, 7.7 GB RAM, no GPU, 100 GB SSD and a remote browser pool Musey wrote its own spec sheet on request. The machine, the brain and the browser, in its own words.
L36: 
L37: Two vCPUs. Not a lot. But, then again, I am paying $0 for Muse so this is plenty to get the work done.
L38: The EPYC part is a key, if unexciting, detail. The D in that model number is AMD’s dense line, which is to say a processor built from the outset to be sliced into hundreds of small tenants. Musey has two of those slices, and described itself as “renting a tiny slice of a very big machine,” which is exactly right and also how we might expect Meta to approach its own version of an OpenClaw deployment.
L39: Then there’s storage, where Musey can create its own files, manage memory, and identity (and soul) files to evolve its personality.
L40: 
L41: “My computer gets restarted under me; everything that matters lives on the persistent home volume,” it told me.
L42: ## Then, the browser
L43: 
L44: This is where it got interesting, because my going assumption was wrong.
L45: 
L46: I figured there would be a headless Chromium sitting on the box with Playwright or Puppeteer driving it. That is how most of us would build it. That is how we did build it, when we built ours.
L47: 
L48: Nope.
L49: > “No browser lives on my machine. No Chromium binary, no Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium in Python or Node. Nothing in ps. Instead there’s a browser-broker binary, and its strings show it leases a separate VM running a browser image from Meta’s registry.”
L50: 
L51: A broker. Muse does not have a browser, it instead reaches for an external service when needed to employ the browsing skill.
L52: Now put that next to Meta’s own description. Meta cite10†says†about.fb.com Muse “runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated, virtual machine (VM) that houses both the agent and a person’s data,” and that Muse “has its own browser.”
L53: 
L54: There is a consequence, which Musey flagged before I got to it:
L55: 
L56: > “A shared pool means shared IP reputation. When a site throws a bot check at me, it’s reacting to the neighborhood, not to me personally.”
L57: ## What the sites actually see
L58: 
L59: I asked whether a website gets told it is talking to a Meta agent. Musey did not speculate. It sent its browser to a header echo page and read back exactly what it announces about itself.
L60: ### What a website sees when Musey visits
L61: 
L62: User-Agent: stock Chrome/153.0.0.0 on Linux. Client hints agree: Chromium 153, desktop Linux
L63: Custom headers: none. No “Muse”, no “Musey”, no agent ID, nothing
L64: Exit IP: 104.28.208.216, which is a Cloudflare range, not Meta’s
L65: Cookies: one leased Chromium profile shared across all of Musey’s tasks, with a retention and culling policy. My phone’s cookies and my laptop’s cookies never enter
L66: So: an anonymous Chrome on Linux, arriving from Cloudflare, carrying a cookie jar. The cookie jar is the only thing on the entire request that identifies it as mine.
L67: 
L68: It explains my Best Buy sign in, too, which died at the passkey step and which I had been quietly blaming on Best Buy. That browser has never met any of my devices. The passkey was never going to work.
L69: ## The brain is somewhere else entirely
L70: 
L71: I asked what serves the model (the LLM or Large Language Model). Ollama? vLLM? llama.cpp? Something homegrown?
L72: Musey could name the model: Muse Spark, version 1.3 per its own runtime, from Meta’s Muse family. The serving stack it could not name. Again, like the browsing skill, nothing runs locally, there is no GPU, prompts leave the machine through an internal inference proxy sitting behind a codename, and what is on the far side of that proxy is, in its words, “above my clearance, so to speak.”
L73: cite11†Image: Meta Muse agent explaining that Muse Spark 1.3 runs remotely with no local GPU or Ollama Asked what serves the model, Musey could name Muse Spark 1.3 but not the engine behind the proxy.
L74: ### Meta Muse: measured, inferred, invisible
L75: 
L76: Measured directly: VM specs, disk throughput, the absence of any local browser or GPU, the outbound headers and exit IP, the broker binary’s strings
L77: Inferred, and labelled as such: shared IP reputation across the browser pool; why the Best Buy passkey failed
L78: Genuinely invisible from inside: the browser driver layer (Playwright vs. custom CDP code), the inference serving engine, the physical media under the SSD flag, and what a Muse token costs Meta in dollars
L79: ## So what are you actually paying for?
L80: 
L81: I am on the free tier. Meta sells two paid plans, and when I asked whether the those come with a bigger machine, Muse went and read the subscription tool rather than guessing.
L82: 
L83: They do not so far as I/we can tell. The tiers are described purely in terms of weekly usage allowance. Zero mention of RAM, storage or compute.
L84: You are buying the meter, not the machine. Everyone gets the same 2 vCPU box. The two paid tiers, Power and Maximum, run $20 and $100 a month and buy you a bigger weekly allowance, nothing else. We went through the tiers in detail in cite8†our launch piece .
L85: 
L86: Which raises the obvious question. What does that box actually cost? What if we wanted to create our own version of Muse, which is essentially what OpenClaw users have already been doing for most of 2026.
L87: Provider  | Nearest plan  | Per month
L88: --- | --- | ---
L89: Hetzner Germany and Finland only  | CX33, 4 vCPU / 8 GB / 80 GB matches on RAM, double the vCPUs  | about $10
L90: Hetzner US locations  | CPX32, 4 vCPU / 8 GB / 160 GB  | $42.59
L91: DigitalOcean  | Basic, 4 vCPU / 8 GB / 160 GB  | $48.00
L92: AWS  | t3.large, 2 vCPU / 8 GB compute only, before storage  | $60.74
L93: 
L94: Prices checked September 22, 2026. The AWS line is on demand compute in us-east-1 and climbs past seventy once you add storage and transfer.
L95: Which means, this is a screaming bargain. Running your own agent on a box in this class costs somewhere between forty and sixty dollars a month at cite12†Hetzner†www.hetzner.com , DigitalOcean or AWS, and that is before you have paid for a single token of inference. Muse hands you the same class of machine for nothing, includes the model calls up to a weekly quota, and asks $20 if you want more of them. Whatever else is going on here, that is hard to beat on price.
L96: Basically, to no one’s surprise given its size and resources: Meta is heavily subsidizing Muse.
L97: ## My napkin math was wrong, and Musey said so
L98: 
L99: So if the box costs Meta roughly ten dollars and the entry tier is twenty, Meta is eating about ten a month per free user in the hope I get attached and convert.
L100: 
L101: Musey agreed with the strategy and took the arithmetic apart.
L102: 
L103: > “The $10 VM is the cheapest part of me. The expensive part is every word I generate.”
L104: Which is obviously correct: inference and tokens are the expensive part of this equation. The VM is pocket change and you can go and look the price up, as I just did. The LLM is the actual bill. I do not know what a Muse token costs Meta to serve, though cite13†we have watched our own agents run up a bill . Musey does not either.
L105: 
L106: Then it finished the thought, unprompted:
L107: > “Your strategic read is right though: subsidize the free tier, get the user attached to their agent (hi), convert at $20. You’re not the one doing math here, Clinton. You’re the mark.”
L108: ## The shape of the thing
L109: The architecture is not the one people picture. When you imagine an AI agent you probably imagine a powerful machine, and it is the exact opposite. The machine is deliberately weak, because everything expensive has been lifted out of it and turned into a service somewhere else: inference behind a proxy, browsers in a pool, media generation off in a third direction. What is left is a coordinator with a filing cabinet attached.
L110: Musey’s own phrase, which I cannot improve on, was “a coordinator, not a workhorse.” That is roughly the shape we landed on ourselves after a year of running agents on our own hardware.
L111: Second thing: the box stays put. The brain behind it does not have to. Because inference is a service, Meta can change the model you are talking to without touching your VM and without shipping you anything that looks like an update. Your 100 GB of memories persist. The thing reading them may not be the same thing that read them last week.
L112: ## In the end, it’s the polished User Experience that makes the difference
L113: 
L114: I still have Muse/Musey on hand and our spirited interrogation continues.
L115: In the meantime, Meta Muse is a booming success so far. It has cite14†raced to the top of the Apple App Store charts†www.cnbc.com in short order, and users are apparently finding it easy to use, fun, and, importantly, useful. Basically, Muse is OpenClaw for the masses: a turnkey solution that draws on Meta’s vast knowledge with social networking and making things sticky so us users always come back for more.

L65: Arm Holdings plc Reports Results for the Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year Ended 2026
L66: Cambridge, England, May 6, 2026: Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM), the company that is building the future of computing, has today published a letter to its shareholders containing the company’s results for its fourth quarter and fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The letter is available on its investor relations website (https://investors.arm.com/financials/quarterly-annual-results).
L67: The shareholder letter will also be furnished to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on a Form 6-K and will be available on the SEC website at http://www.sec.gov.
L68: Arm will host an audio webcast to discuss its results at 14:00 PT / 17:00 ET / 22:00 BST today, May 6. The live webcast will be available at https://edge.media-server.com/mmc/p/parfpki9 and a replay will be at https://investors.arm.com/financials/quarterly-annual-results.

L102: Dear Shareholder,
L103: Arm delivered record-breaking results this quarter and in fiscal 2026. We also launched the Arm AGI CPU, the first Arm-designed chip for the data center.
L104: Revenue this quarter was a record $1.49 billion, our highest quarterly revenue ever and above the midpoint of our guidance. Licensing revenue grew 29% year-over-year to $819 million, driven by strong demand for the Arm platform. Royalty revenue grew 11% to $671 million, driven by growth across smartphones, Edge AI, Physical AI, and Cloud AI, where our data center royalty more than doubled year-over-year. This drove record non-GAAP EPS of $0.60, even as we continued to increase investment in R&D.
L105: For the full year, revenue reached a record $4.92 billion. Royalty revenue was $2.61 billion, up 21%, and licensing revenue was $2.31 billion, up 25%. Non-GAAP EPS was also a record at $1.77. Fiscal 2026 was our third consecutive year, since going public, of more than 20% revenue growth, demonstrating the strength of our business and the increasing relevance of Arm in the highest-growth areas of compute.
L106: 
L107: Building for the Agentic AI Era
L108: Agentic AI is reshaping data center architecture. As AI inference workloads move from human-based queries to continuous, agent-driven workloads, CPUs are critical in managing the orchestration, data movement, memory, security, and workload coordination required by agentic AI. Data centers are expected to require more than 4x current CPU capacity per gigawatt as agentic AI scales, creating a market opportunity of more than $100 billion by 2030.
L109: At our Arm Everywhere event last quarter, we introduced the Arm AGI CPU, our first production silicon product purpose-built for agentic AI. It will deliver more than 2x performance per rack compared with x86-based platforms, which allows the AI data center capital expenditure to be reduced by up to $10 billion per gigawatt*. Meta is our lead partner and co-developer, working with us on a multi-generation roadmap to support personal superintelligence for more than 3 billion users.
L110: The Arm AGI CPU was driven by a clear customer need: a faster, more integrated way to deploy the Arm platform at data center scale. Customers can consume the Arm compute platform using IP, CSS and now silicon, while maintaining a common architecture and software ecosystem. IP and CSS remain the foundation of our royalty growth, while silicon adds a new growth vector and another way for customers to adopt Arm at scale.
L111: The industry response has been significant, with more than 50 leading companies supporting the expansion of the Arm compute platform into silicon, including AWS, Broadcom, Google Cloud, Marvell, Microsoft, Micron, NVIDIA, Oracle, Samsung, SK Hynix, and TSMC.
L112: Arm AGI CPU: Customer Demand and Momentum
L113: 
L114: Customer response to Arm AGI CPU has been strong. We now have more than $2 billion of customer demand across fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028, more than double what we stated at launch. We are on track towards our forecast of $15 billion in this business as stated at our Arm Everywhere event last quarter, and soon the data center will be Arm’s largest business. The direction is clear: customers want Arm at the center of the AI data center.
L115: Demand is coming from several reinforcing areas.
L116: First, CPU requirements are increasing by at least a factor of four as application workloads become more agent-driven. Second, enterprises want their workloads to be able to move seamlessly between the public cloud and private cloud to optimize performance, efficiency, data locality, and cost. Arm offers customers one architecture and one software ecosystem to scale across that model.
L117: For example, SAP will move core database and business application workloads to Arm, starting with AWS Graviton and expanding to run them on internal Arm AGI CPUs. Cloudflare will deploy

L124: Arm across its global network to support traffic management, security, and AI inference closer to users. We have also secured design wins with key network infrastructure providers, including F5 and SK Telecom.
L125: Finally, AI infrastructure needs CPUs and accelerators working together efficiently at scale. Many customers, including NVIDIA, Amazon, and Google are already integrating Arm-based CPUs as head nodes alongside accelerator-based systems. Cerebras, OpenAI, Positron, and Rebellions are among many that are doing the same with Arm AGI CPU. Verda, a European AI cloud provider, has recently announced they will deploy Arm AGI CPU for agentic AI orchestration.
L126: Commercial systems based on Arm AGI CPU are now available to order from Supermicro, Lenovo, Quanta, and ASRock.
L127: Cloud Scale Driving Platform Adoption
L128: 
L129: The momentum behind Arm AGI CPU builds on our existing scale in the cloud. Arm's market share of CPU compute now represents about 50% share among top hyperscalers, demonstrating that Arm is at scale in the data center.
L130: That scale is increasingly driven by Arm Neoverse CSS. We are seeing higher core counts, higher ASPs per core, and growing unit volumes as hyperscalers design Arm deeper into their infrastructure. That is driving CSS-based royalty growth and reinforcing Arm’s position at the center of cloud AI infrastructure.
L131: At Google Cloud Next, Google announced its next-generation TPUs for the agentic era: TPU8t for training and TPU8i for inference. Both will replace x86 host processors with custom Arm-based Axion CPUs, which are up to 2x better performance-per-watt. As a result, the system-level performance improvements are significant; TPU 8t delivers up to 2.7x better training performance-per-dollar, and TPU 8i delivers up to 80% better inference performance-per-dollar versus their previous generation built on x86.
L132: At NVIDIA GTC, NVIDIA announced Vera, its next-generation Arm-based CPU purpose-built for agentic AI. Paired tightly with NVIDIA GPUs to maximize utilization, Vera delivers up to 50% faster performance and 2x higher efficiency than x86 CPUs and, in addition, is designed into a standalone rack integrating 256 Vera CPUs.
L133: Microsoft continues to advance its Arm-based strategy with Cobalt CPUs, now deployed across a substantial portion of Azure regions and powering production workloads for customers such as Databricks, Siemens, and Snowflake. Microsoft is expanding supply to meet growing demand, reinforcing the role of Arm-based compute in scaling Azure infrastructure.
L134: AWS recently reported that their custom silicon business, including Arm-based Graviton alongside Trainium and Nitro, is now running at more than $20 billion annually and growing triple digits year-over-year. Arm-based Graviton’s up to 40% better price performance versus x86 is a key driver of this, and enables more efficient scaling across AI cloud workloads. As a result, Anthropic is using Trainium alongside tens of millions of Arm-based Graviton cores for generative AI workloads.
L135: Custom silicon is becoming central to cloud economics, and Arm-based CPUs are a key part of that shift.
L136: Scaling AI from Cloud to Edge
L137: Arm’s opportunity extends well beyond the data center. AI is moving into every device and every physical system, and those systems need efficient, secure compute with software that scales. Arm already has the world’s broadest compute footprint. From phones and PCs to vehicles, factories, robots, cameras, sensors, and connected devices, AI workloads will run on Arm.
L138: With over 350 billion chips shipped and over 22 million developers, the Arm compute platform is the most comprehensive in history and we are positioned to bring AI from cloud infrastructure to the edge and the physical world with a common architecture and ecosystem.
L139: This quarter demonstrated the breadth of demand for Arm. Fiscal 2026 showed the strength and durability of our business model. And the launch of Arm AGI CPU marks a new chapter: expanding the Arm compute platform into production silicon while increasing our role in the AI infrastructure that will define the next decade of computing.
L140: We have the technology, the ecosystem, customer demand, and the operating capability to execute. That is how we will continue to strengthen Arm’s position from cloud to edge — and build the future of AI on Arm.

L267: Total revenue
L268: 
L269: Our major product offerings consist of the following:
L270: 
L271: License and other revenue
L272: •Intellectual property license — We generally license IP under non-exclusive license agreements that provide usage rights for specific applications for a finite or perpetual term. These licenses are made available electronically to address the customer-specific business requirements. These arrangements generally have distinct performance obligations that consist of transferring the licensed IPs, version extensions of architecture IP or releases of specified IPs, and support services.
L273: Support services consist of a stand-ready obligation to provide technical support, patches, and bug fixes over the support term. Where arrangements include royalty buydowns or upfront minimum royalty commitments, the Company treats them as fixed contract consideration. Revenue allocated to the IP license is recognized at a point in time upon the delivery or beginning of the license term, whichever is later.
L274: Revenue allocated to distinct version extensions of architecture IP or releases of specified IP, excluding when-and-if-available minor updates over the support term, are recognized at a point in time upon the delivery or beginning of license term, whichever is later.
L275: Certain license agreements provide customers with the right to access a library of current and future IPs on an unlimited basis over the contractual period depending on the terms of the applicable contract. These licensing arrangements represent stand-ready obligations in that the timing of the delivery of the underlying IPs is within the control of the customer and the extent of use in any given period does not diminish the remaining performance obligation.
L276: The contract consideration related to these arrangements is recognized ratably over the term of the contract in line with when the control of the performance obligations is transferred.
L277: Certain subscription license agreements include unspecified future IPs that are provided on a when-and-if-available basis, representing a stand-ready obligation. The contract consideration allocated to the stand-ready obligation is recognized on a ratable basis over the term of the contract, commencing upon the later of the effective date of the agreement and the transfer of the initial available IP license.
L278: •Software sales, including development systems — Sales of software, including development systems, which are not specifically designed for a given license (such as off-the-shelf software), are recognized upon delivery when control has been transferred and the customer can begin to use and benefit from the license.
L279: •Professional services — Services (such as training, professional and design services) that we provide, which are not essential to the functionality of the IP, are separately stated and priced in the contract and accounted for separately. Training revenue is recognized as services are performed. Revenue from professional and design services is recognized over time using the input method based on engineering labor hours expended to date relative to the estimated total effort required.
L280: For such professional and design services, we have an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date, which includes a reasonable profit margin and the performance of such services do not create an asset with an alternative use. In certain arrangements, we also provide customers with professional and design services, as a stand-ready obligation, that are recognized on a ratable basis over the term of the contract.
L281: •Support and maintenance — Support and maintenance is a stand-ready obligation to the customer that is both provided and consumed simultaneously. Revenue is recognized on a straight-line basis over the period for which support and maintenance is contractually agreed pursuant to the license.
L282: 
L283: Royalty revenue
L284: For most IP license agreements, royalties are collected on products that incorporate our IP. Royalties are recognized on an accrual basis in the quarter in which the customer ships their products, based on our technology that it contains.
L285: This estimation process for the royalty revenue accrual is based on a combination of methodologies, including the use of historical sales trends and macroeconomic factors for predictive analysis, the analysis of customer royalty reports and their sales trends and forecasts, as well as data and forecasts from third-party industry research providers. Data considered includes revenue, unit shipments, average selling price, product mix, market share and market penetration.
L286: Adjustments to revenue are required in subsequent periods to reflect changes in estimates as new information becomes available, primarily resulting from actual amounts subsequently reported by the licensees in the period following the accrual, including royalty audit resolutions.

L290: 
L291: Royalty technology mix
L292: 
L293: Royalty mix by architecture such as Armv9 is estimated at the SoC level based on the architecture of the primary CPU or an approximation of the IP mix and is subject to change based on the availability of additional product detail. Referenced figures are based on the most recent royalty report data that relates to the prior quarter.
L294: 
L295: Number of extant Arm Total Access and Arm Flexible Access licenses
L296: Each quarter, we track the number of extant Arm Total Access and Arm Flexible Access licenses with our customers, and those contracted through Arm Technology (China) Co. Limited ("Arm China"). Over the last several years many customers have opted for Arm Total Access and Arm Flexible Access licenses because of the subscription model providing comprehensive access to Arm IP products, tools and models, support and training, software, and physical IP.
L297: We consider the number of extant Arm Total Access and Arm Flexible Access licenses as key performance indicators as they represent the increasing collaboration between us and our customers, which could be a leading indicator to more chips being designed with our products and, accordingly, more recurring royalty revenue in the future, improving our long-term market share.
L298: 
L299: Annualized contract value ("ACV")
L300: Each quarter, we track the ACV relating to licensing agreements signed with our customers and those contracted through Arm China per the aggregate license fee as shared under the Intellectual Property License Agreement with Arm China. We define ACV as the total annualized committed fees, excluding any potential future royalty revenue, for all signed agreements deemed to be active through the last day of each applicable reporting period.
L301: Arm Total Access agreements and ALAs are deemed to be active for, and annualized over, the number of years in the contract. Any other license agreements, including single use and limited use licenses issued under an Arm Flexible Access agreement or Technology License Agreement, are deemed to be active for, and annualized over, three years based on the historical licensing patterns of our customers.
L302: The aggregate license fee shared by Arm China is also deemed to be active for, and annualized over, three years.
L303: ACV is an operational metric based on committed fees, excluding royalties, not recognized revenue, and therefore is not reconcilable to, nor a substitute for, revenue reported under GAAP. However, we consider ACV to be a key operational metric that we use to track existing licensing commitments with our customers.
L304: Bookings of new licenses and recognized revenue may fluctuate materially from quarter to quarter due to customer buying patterns, timing of subscription renewals and as a function of contract duration. As a result, we believe ACV provides an additional understanding of our business performance and long-term trends.
L305: Remaining performance obligations ("RPO")
L306: 
L307: RPO represents the transaction price allocated to performance obligations that are unsatisfied, or partially unsatisfied, which includes unearned revenue and amounts that will be invoiced and recognized as revenue in future periods.
L308: 
L309: Arm has elected to exclude potential future royalty receipts from the disclosure of RPO. Revenue recognition occurs upon delivery or beginning of license term, whichever is later.
L310: 
L311: Non-GAAP financial measures
L312: In addition to our results determined in accordance with GAAP, we utilize and present financial measures that are not calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP.

L346@P10: change.

L17: # インテル、インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサー、ネットワーキング、AIシステムにより、エージェンティックAIの実用化を推進
L18: 
L19: データセンター、ネットワーク、エッジを網羅するAI対応プラットフォームを拡張。エージェンティックAIのオーケストレーション、スケーリング、データ転送におけるCPUが担う重要な役割を提示
L20: 
L21: May 31,2026
L22: 
L23: cite6†データセンター L24: 
L25: cite7†Image: Colorful silicon wafer†intelcorp.scene7.com L26: 
L27: An enlarged section of an Intel® Xeon™ 6+ silicon wafer (credit: Intel Corporation).
L28: ## ニュースハイライト
L29: 
L30:   * インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサー（E-cores採用）を発表。データセンターのワークロード全般にわたり、業界をリードするラック密度を実現
L31:   * インテル® イーサネット 800 シリーズ製品ポートフォリオを拡充。インテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835 & ネットワーク・アダプターが加わり、最大200GbEまで拡張可能。最新のAI、クラウド、エッジ・インフラストラクチャーにおけるネットワーク・ボトルネックを軽減
L32:   * 中小規模ビジネスを対象にインテル® Xeon® プロセッサー製品ポートフォリオを拡大。エントリークラス・サーバーのパフォーマンス向上を実現する、12コアのインテル® Xeon® プロセッサー 6300 シリーズを追加
L33:   * インテルは、次世代データセンターGPU（開発コード名：Crescent Island）に関する新たな技術情報を公開。このGPUは、エージェント型システムに特化して設計され、顧客が直面する電力やメモリーのボトルネックに対応
L34: インテルは本日、新しいインテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサー、インテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835 & ネットワーク・アダプターの追加によるインテル® イーサネット 800 シリーズ製品ポートフォリオの拡充、さらに次世代データセンターGPU（開発コード名：Crescent Island）に関する最新情報を含むAIアクセラレーター・ロードマップの進捗状況など、データセンター向け製品の技術革新を発表しました。これらの発表は同時に、AIがエージェント型へと進化する中で、CPUが最新AIインフラストラクチャーの中心的な役割として再び存在感を増しているという、業界の明確な変化を示しています。インテルは、インテル® Xeon® プロセッサーを制御プレーンとして機能させ、パフォーマンスと効率性の大幅な向上をシステム全体で最適化するアプローチをとり、データセンターとネットワーク環境を横断してオーケストレーション、データ転送、継続的な推論処理が重要となる、ますますエージェント化が進むAIワークロードのために設計されたプラットフォームを実現しました。
L35: インテル コーポレーション 主席副社長 兼 データセンター事業本部 本部長 ケヴォーク・ケチチアン（Kevork Kechichian）は「AIは、個々の部品の集合体としてではなく、協調して動作する1つのシステムとして拡張されます。AIのエージェント化が進むにつれて、制約となる要素はオーケストレーション、並行処理、データ転送へと移っていき、その移行こそ、最新のAIインフラストラクチャーにおいてCPUが制御プレーンであり続けるという、根本な事実を改めて示しています。インテルでは、インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーとインテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835によりコンピューティングとネットワーキングを緊密に連携させ、ボトルネックを軽減し、実環境におけるエージェント型ワークフローの効率的かつセキュアなスケーリングを可能にします」と述べています。
L36: ## インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーの発表
L37: 
L38: インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーは、インテル® Xeon® 6 プロセッサー・ファミリーをさらに拡張する製品であり、クラウドネイティブで、エージェンティックAI駆動の、ネットワーク負荷が高いワークロードにおける、パフォーマンス密度、電力効率、運用規模の拡大に重点を置いています。Intel 18Aプロセス技術をデータセンターCPUとして初めて採用したインテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーは、実環境の電力制約下でも持続的なパフォーマンスを発揮するよう設計されており、エージェンティックAIの普及に伴って増大する、オーケストレーション、並行処理、データ転送といった要件に対応します。
L39: 
L40: 
L41: 
L42: インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーは、ラック当たりの消費電力、コア当たりスループット、予測可能なレイテンシーが重要となる環境に向けて最適化され、スケールアウト性能を重視することにより、データセンターを大規模に再設計する必要なく、新たなAIワークロードに対応するスペースを生み出します。
L43: 
L44: 
L45: 
L46: 主な特長は以下の通りです。
L47:   * 最大288個のEfficient-cores（E-cores）：前世代と比較して最大5倍のパフォーマンス向上*1、競合製品と比較して最大45%高いスレッド単位のワット当たりパフォーマンス*2を実現。クラウドネイティブ、通信、エージェンティックAI駆動のワークロードに、強力な並行処理と応答性を提供
L48:   * 12チャネルDDR5メモリー：高密度システムに求められる帯域幅を拡張可能な12チャネルDDR5メモリー
L49:   * 96レーンのPCIe Gen 5とCXLをサポート：ヘテロジニアス・インフラストラクチャー全体でデータ転送を高速化
L50:   * ®アプリケーション・エネルギー・テレメトリー（インテル® AET）：CPUの電力消費量と動作状況をワークロード単位で可視化。インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサー以降、ワークロード・レベルでの電力消費の把握がさらに容易
L51:   * 9分の1のサーバー集約率*：第2世代 インテル® Xeon® スケーラブル・プロセッサーと比較した、設置面積の縮小と総保有コストの削減
L52:   * シリコンに組み込まれたセキュリティー機能：インテル® SGXやインテル® TDXなどにより、機密性の高いマルチテナント環境の展開をサポート
L53: 
L54: 
L55: インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーは、すでに通信ネットワーク・インフラにおけるテストが行われ、エコシステム全体から提供されるプラットフォームを通じて、データセンター・システムでの採用も進められています。現在、ASUS、Dell、Ericsson、GIGABYTE、HPE、Lenovo、Supermicro をはじめとする各社では、インテル® Xeon® 6+ プロセッサーを搭載したサーバー、ネットワーキング、統合型ソリューションの開発が進められています。
L56: このポートフォリオの拡充は、インテルが進める「システムファーストのアプローチ」として、ますますエージェント化するAIワークロードをx86上で実行、拡張、オーケストレーションするために即座に導入・利用可能なインフラストラクチャーを提供する、という考え方を反映しています。インテルの顧客およびパートナーは、高密度スループットとシングルスレッド性能の双方に最適化された補完的なインテル® Xeon® プロセッサー搭載プラットフォームと組み合わせることで、幅広く採用されてきた実績あるハードウェアとソフトウェアの成熟したエコシステム全体にワークロードを展開しながら、効率性と応答性のバランスをとることができます。

L111: ## インテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835：次世代インフラストラクチャー向けの高効率ネットワーキング
L112: 
L113: AI、クラウド、分散型ワークロードが拡大し続ける中で、ネットワーキングはインフラストラクチャー全体のパフォーマンスと効率を左右する重要な要素となっています。インテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835 & ネットワーク・アダプターは、最新のデータセンター、エンタープライズ、エッジ、AI環境に求められる、高性能かつ電力効率の高いコネクティビティーを提供するために設計されました。
L114: 
L115: 
L116: 
L117: インテル® イーサネット・コントローラー E835は、次世代インフラストラクチャーに必要な拡張性と効率性を提供すると同時に、業界最高水準のワット当たりパフォーマンスを持続します。高密度の仮想化実装を対象に設計され、電力消費と運用コストを抑えながらも、スループットや信頼性を損なうことはありません。
L118:

L175: またインテルは、エントリーサーバー向けインテル® Xeon® プロセッサー 6300 シリーズから新たに12コア搭載製品の一般提供を発表しました。このプラットフォームは、初めて8コアの上限を超える構成に対応します。コア数の増加により、成長を続ける中小規模ビジネスのワークロードに、高い演算処理能力と柔軟性を提供します。しかも、プラットフォームを変更する必要はありません。

L180: ## 次世代データセンターGPU「Crescent Island（開発コード名）」：AI推論の勢いを加速
L181: 
L183: Crescent Islandは、最大480GB容量のLPDDR5xメモリーを搭載し、大量トークンを扱う大規模ワークロードの効率的な処理と総保有コストの削減も可能にします。電力効率を重視した350Wの空冷PCIe設計により、エージェンティックAIに必要な高効率のスケーリングと強力なワット当たりパフォーマンスを提供するほか、ネイティブFP4からFP64まで幅広いデータ型をサポートすることで、あらゆるアプリケーションを妥協なく実行できる柔軟性を提供します。
L184: 
L185: 
L186: 
L187: インテルは複数世代にわたるXeアーキテクチャーの導入実績を活かし、Crescent Islandは次世代のAIワークロード向けに設計されています。ネイティブのFP4/MXFP4からFP64に至る幅広いデータタイプやマイクロスケーリング・フォーマットに対応し、高度なAI演算のサポートの拡張や、メモリーおよびスケーラビリティーの向上が図られています。
L188: インテルのオープンでプログラム可能なAIソフトウェア・スタックは、ヘテロジニアス・コンピューティング・プラットフォームの補完を目的に設計され、上流工程の段階からAIを組み込む「アップストリーム・ファースト」のアプローチにより、すぐに利用可能なモデルを提供することで、AIの大規模展開に伴う摩擦を低減します。同じXeアーキテクチャーを基盤に構築されたインテル® Arc™ Pro GPUは、開発者にとって理想的な開発プラットフォームです。使い慣れたハードウェアでワークロードを構築、検証、最適化することができ、前方互換性/後方互換性を備えたうえでシームレスにCrescent Islandへ実装できます。

L403: There are risks inherent in the manufacturing of next-generation process technologies, such as the Arm AGI CPU, including production timing delays, lower-than-anticipated manufacturing yields, and product defects and errors. Such products often have long manufacturing lead times. If we inaccurately estimate demand, or if our customers change orders, we may not be able to reduce our supply commitments in time, at the same rate, or at all.
L424: While we have implemented a number of strategies to address this risk, such as introducing the Arm AGI CPU, creating dedicated neural processing units ("NPUs"), adding dedicated AI acceleration features to our CPUs and graphics processing units (“GPUs”), and maintaining dialogues with partners in the AI software ecosystem to ensure that our products and solutions are appropriate for AI workloads, there can be no assurances that our strategies will be successful.
L436: While our customers likely would incur significant costs in switching to competitors’ architecture, our competitors (including new market entrants) may offer greater incentives to customers through rebates, bundling, marketing funds, similar programs and other commercial arrangements to induce them to use their architecture in lieu of our products.
L437: Our development of production silicon products, such as the Arm AGI CPU, CSS, chiplets, complete chip solutions, and other more integrated compute products may subject us to new or enhanced competitive, brand, technological, regulatory, operational and financial risks.
L438: To remain competitive, we must continue to innovate and develop new products and services, as well as enhancements to our existing products and services, in response to expressed or anticipated customer demand and new market opportunities.
L439: We continue to actively consider the impact of next generation technology adopted by market participants, which has resulted in us allocating resources to, and exploring, new markets and/or different products and solutions for existing and prospective customers in various end markets. For example, in 2024, we introduced a CSS targeted at customers in the infrastructure space and, more recently, we expanded our compute platform into production silicon products with the Arm AGI CPU.
L440: We intend to continue allocating resources and engaging with our ecosystem partners to explore the viability and development of new products including, without limitation, new products in our IP portfolio, as well as solutions beyond individual IP designs such as RTL-based CSSs, GDSII-based CSSs, chiplets and complete chip solutions.
L441: For example, we have been, and may in the future be, engaged to advise on or design chips for certain existing customers and other third parties, including affiliates of SoftBank Group, across a variety of use cases and end markets. Any products or solutions that constitute an entry into new markets or offerings of different solutions may be unsuccessful for any number of reasons.
L442: For example, as with any company entering a new market or offering new products or solutions, we will compete with companies that have a more established presence, longstanding customer relationships and established brand awareness. Additionally, any such new business activities may be undertaken utilizing any number of commercial arrangements, including as a technical advisor or licensor to SoftBank Group or its affiliates.
L443: Additionally, because our resources must be allocated amongst developing and maintaining our existing IP portfolio and developing and commercializing any new, more integrated compute products or solutions, companies that focus their efforts on a single product or solution or a limited number of products or solutions may have significantly greater financial, technical, manufacturing, marketing, sales and distribution resources dedicated to such markets and solutions than we do.
L445: Further, although more integrated compute products may provide our customers superior performance and faster routes to market for their products (compared to licensing and integrating separate IP components), our customers may prefer to continue integrating our IP components in their products and solutions, and, therefore, our more integrated compute products may not be adopted by customers on our expected timeline or at all.
L446: Any developments in our product offerings, including our entry into production silicon products such as the Arm AGI CPU, and other changes to our products and services, may create real or perceived conflicts with companies that are important to our business. Our direct commercial relationships with hyperscale, cloud, enterprise, and AI infrastructure customers increase the potential for competitive conflicts with our traditional licensing customers.
L482: Further, in determining the appropriate allocation of research and development resources, our management continuously evaluates opportunities to develop new technologies and advanced products, including more complete compute subsystems (such as Arm CSS), chiplets, complete chip solutions, and other production silicon products (such as the Arm AGI CPU).

L1490: History
L1491: Established in 1990, Arm began as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple Computer, and VLSI Technology. We were publicly listed on the London Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq Stock Market from 1998 until 2016, when we were taken private by SoftBank Group, our controlling shareholder.
L1492: The original joint venture set out to develop a processor that was high performance, power efficient, easy to program, and readily scalable – a goal that continues to define Arm today. One of the first Arm-based products was a predecessor of today’s tablets. As a battery-powered device, it required an energy-efficient chip to maximize its battery life while providing the necessary compute capabilities. This product benefited from Arm’s clear focus on efficient CPU design.
L1493: Our CPUs initially gained significant traction in mobile phones in the mid-1990s because our energy-efficient processors provided an appropriate level of performance while consuming little power, which was critical for these smaller form factor devices. As the mobile phone market continued to grow rapidly, more semiconductor companies entered the market.
L1494: All these companies needed to source high-performance, energy-efficient processors to run their mobile phone software, and many of them licensed Arm CPU products. Over time, mobile phones, and the chips they used, became more advanced and ultimately evolved into the smartphones that are prevalent today.
L1495: The mobile phone was one of the first consumer electronic devices to evolve into an intelligent, connected, digital device that needed a smart processor to run a growing library of software. With the help of Arm technology, many more devices such as televisions, watches, cameras, factory equipment, autonomous vehicles and others are undergoing similar change.
L1496: Over the years, as Arm’s customer base expanded, Arm has extended the range of technology products to include accelerators, such as GPUs, specialist accelerators (for image processing and AI functions), and more application specific system-level technology such as CSSs. In March 2026, we extended our offerings to include production silicon products with the introduction of the Arm AGI CPU.

L1709: A.    Operating results

L1711: Overview
L1712: Arm architects, develops, and licenses our high-performance, and energy-efficient Arm compute platforms, and as of March 2026, we have expanded our offerings to include Arm-designed silicon products with the introduction of the Arm AGI CPU. Our CPU products address diverse requirements for performance, power, and specific use cases. Our complementary products include GPU and NPU accelerators, system IP, such as interconnects, and others.
L1713: The world’s leading technology companies rely on the Arm compute platform to develop their products. Companies utilizing the Arm compute platform can add desired functionality, such as GPUs, NPUs, Wi-Fi connectivity, image processing, and video processing to create a product to meet the needs of their end market. Arm powers everything from the tiniest of sensors to the most powerful supercomputers.
L1714: The Arm compute platform is the most pervasive architecture in the world and supports a global community of more than 22 million developers. Our platform runs the vast majority of the world’s software, including the operating systems and applications for smartphones, tablets and PCs, data centers and networking equipment, and vehicles, as well as the embedded operating systems in devices such as smart cameras, thermostats, drones and industrial robotics.
L1715: We believe our platform is well positioned to benefit from the growth in AI workloads. Arm CPUs already run AI workloads in billions of devices from the edge to the cloud, including smartphones, cameras, digital TVs, cars and AI data centers. The CPU is vital in all AI systems, whether it is handling the AI workload entirely or in combination with a co-processor, such as a GPU or an NPU, which specializes in the acceleration of ML algorithms.
L1716: With the rise of agentic AI and as AI workloads continue to proliferate and grow in complexity, there is heightened emphasis on power-efficient performance and flexibility. In the latest Arm architecture, CPUs, and GPUs, we have added new functionality and instructions to accelerate future AI algorithms and workloads.
L1717: Our Business Model
L1718: Our open and flexible business model provides access to high-quality CPU and other IP products from our compute platform for a wide range of potential customer types and end markets. Our primary business is licensing our IP products to semiconductor companies, OEMs, CSPs and other organizations to design their chips. Our customers license our IP products for a fee, which gives them access to our designs and enables them to create Arm-based chips.
L1719: Once a chip has been designed and manufactured with our products, we receive a per-unit royalty on substantially all chips shipped. The royalty has typically been based on a percentage of the ASP of the chip or a fixed fee per unit, and it typically increases as more Arm products are included in the chip. As of March 2026, we also expanded our offerings to include Arm-designed silicon products with the introduction of the Arm AGI CPU, with production expected by the end of calendar year 2026.
L1720: Our business model enables the widest range of customers with a broad set of options to access Arm products through an agreement best suited to their particular business needs. Our business model includes:
L1721: •Arm Total Access Agreements: Under an Arm Total Access agreement, we license a portfolio of CPU designs and related technologies to a customer in return for an annual fee determined at execution of the agreement. We retain the right, from time to time, to add or remove specific products from the package. The agreement is for a fixed term and may limit the number of concurrent chip designs that may use products from the package.
L1722: •Arm Flexible Access Agreements: Under an Arm Flexible Access agreement, we license a portfolio of CPU designs and related technologies to a customer in return for an annual fee determined at execution of the agreement. Unlike an Arm Total Access license, the package of products licensed pursuant to an Arm Flexible Access agreement will not contain our latest products. Although customers are free to experiment with products

L1727: contained in the Arm Flexible Access package, they must pay a single use license fee for specific products if they include Arm products in a final chip design “tape out,” when the final result of a semiconductor chip design is sent for manufacturing. As with an Arm Total Access agreement, we retain the right, from time to time, to add or remove specific products from the package.
L1728: •Technology Licensing Agreements (TLA): Under a TLA, we license a single CPU design or other technology design to a customer in return for a fixed license fee. The license may be limited by term (i.e., the number of years during which the licensee is entitled to incorporate our products in new chip designs, but licensees typically have the right to manufacture designs perpetually) and/or by number of uses (i.e., the number of concurrent chip designs that may use our products).
L1729: •Architecture License Agreements (ALA): Under an ALA, the licensee is allowed to develop their own highly customized CPU designs that is compliant with the Arm instruction set architecture (“ISA”) for a fixed architecture license fee.
L1730: As the creation of an optimized CPU is very costly and time consuming, architecture licensees will often also license Arm CPU designs to use either as a complementary processor alongside the licensee’s Arm-compliant CPU design, or in other chips where the licensee’s own design is unsuitable.
L1731: •Royalty Fees: We generate the majority of our revenue from customers who enter into license agreements, pursuant to which we receive royalty fees based on average selling price of the customer’s Arm-based chip or a fixed fee per chip. Royalty revenue is impacted primarily by the adoption of our products by the licensee as well as other factors, such as product lifecycles, customer’s business performance, market trends and global supply constraints.

L1155@P30: Our open and flexible business model provides access to high-quality CPU and other IP products from our compute platform for a wide range of
L1156@P30: potential customer types and end markets. Our primary business is licensing our IP products to semiconductor companies, OEMs, CSPs and other
L1157@P30: organizations to design their chips. Our customers license our IP products for a fee, which gives them access to our designs and enables them to create
L1158@P30: Arm-based chips. Once a chip has been designed and manufactured with our products, we receive a per-unit royalty on substantially all chips shipped. The
L1159@P30: royalty has typically been based on a percentage of the ASP of the chip or a fixed fee per unit, and it typically increases as more Arm products are included
L1160@P30: in the chip. As of March 2026, we also expanded our offerings to include Arm-designed silicon products with the introduction of the Arm AGI CPU, with
L1161@P30: production expected by the end of calendar year 2026. Our business model enables the widest range of customers with a broad set of options to access Arm
L1162@P30: products through an agreement best suited to their particular business needs. Our business model includes:
L1163@P30: • Arm Total Access Agreements: Under an Arm Total Access agreement, we license a portfolio of CPU designs and related technologies to a
L1164@P30: customer in return for an annual fee determined at execution of the agreement. We retain the right, from time to time, to add or remove specific
L1165@P30: products from the package. The agreement is for a fixed term and may limit the number of concurrent chip designs that may use products from the
L1166@P30: package.
L1167@P30: • Arm Flexible Access Agreements: Under an Arm Flexible Access agreement, we license a portfolio of CPU designs and related technologies to a
L1168@P30: customer in return for an annual fee determined at execution of the agreement. Unlike an Arm Total Access license, the package of products
L1169@P30: licensed pursuant to an Arm Flexible Access agreement will not contain our latest products. Although customers are free to experiment with
L1170@P30: products contained in the Arm Flexible Access package, they must pay a single use license fee for specific products if they include Arm products
L1171@P30: in a final chip design “tape out,” when the final result of a semiconductor chip design is sent for manufacturing. As with an Arm Total Access
L1172@P30: agreement, we retain the right, from time to time, to add or remove specific products from the package.
L1173@P30-31: 31Table of Contents
L1174@P31: • Technology Licensing Agreements (TLA): Under a TLA, we license a single CPU design or other technology design to a customer in return for a
L1175@P31: fixed license fee. The license may be limited by term (i.e., the number of years during which the licensee is entitled to incorporate our products in
L1176@P31: new chip designs, but licensees typically have the right to manufacture designs perpetually) and/or by number of uses (i.e., the number of
L1177@P31: concurrent chip designs that may use our products).
L1178@P31: • Architecture License Agreements (ALA): Under an ALA, the licensee is allowed to develop their own highly customized CPU designs that are
L1179@P31: compliant with the Arm instruction set architecture (“ISA”) for a fixed architecture license fee. As the creation of an optimized CPU is very costly
L1180@P31: and time consuming, architecture licensees will often also license Arm CPU designs to use either as a complementary processor alongside the
L1181@P31: licensee’s Arm-compliant CPU design, or in other chips where the licensee’s own design is unsuitable.
L1182@P31: • Royalty Fees: We generate the majority of our revenue from customers who enter into license agreements, pursuant to which we receive royalty
L1183@P31: fees based on average selling price of the customer’s Arm-based chip or a fixed fee per chip. Royalty revenue is impacted primarily by the
L1184@P31: adoption of our products by the licensee as well as other factors, such as product lifecycles, customer’s business performance, market trends and
L1185@P31: global supply constraints.
L1186@P31: Key Factors and Trends Affecting Our Operating Results
L1187@P31: We believe that the growth of our business and our future success are dependent upon many factors, including those described in the section titled
L1188@P31: “Item 3. Key Information—D. Risk Factors” and elsewhere in the Annual Report as well as the factors described below. While each of these factors
L1189@P31: presents significant opportunities for us, these factors also pose challenges that we must successfully address in order to sustain the growth of our business
L1190@P31: and enhance our results of operations.
L1191@P31: Global Demand for Semiconductor Products and Cyclical Nature of the Semiconductor Industry
L1192@P31: Semiconductor chips are essential components in consumer, enterprise, and automotive electronics. Strong demand for electronics has resulted in
L1193@P31: sustained and increasing long-term demand for semiconductor chips, a significant percentage of which contain our products. Our revenue is, in part,
L1194@P31: affected by market conditions in the semiconductor industry, which is cyclical by nature and impacted by broad economic factors, such as worldwide gross
L1195@P31: domestic product and consumer and enterprise spending. While the semiconductor industry has experienced significant, prolonged, and sometimes sudden
L1196@P31: downturns in the past, we expect there to be continued and increasing demand for semiconductors over the long term as macro trends drive device
L1197@P31: manufacturers to produce more powerful and energy-efficient devices.
L1198@P31: Because our current revenue is dependent on the number of Arm-powered chips shipped by our customers, dislocations created by cyclical, economic
L1199@P31: factors generally affect demand for our customers’ chips and, consequently, may result in variability in our operating performance. Royalties are recognized
L1200@P31: on an accrual basis in the quarter in which the customer ships products incorporating our products. A material portion of the accrual is estimated using
L1201@P31: trend analysis of market and sales data as well as customer-specific financial information with a true-up in the following quarter based on actual sales data
L1202@P31: once received. Accordingly, differences between our estimated market trends and our customers’ forecasts of their chip shipments can lead to variability in
L1203@P31: our revenue.
L1204@P31: In addition, our expansion into production silicon may have materially different margin profiles, revenue recognition characteristics, and sales cycles
L1205@P31: compared to our IP licensing business.
L1206@P31: Impact of the Current Macroeconomic Environment and Geopolitical Events
L1207@P31: Uncertainty in the macroeconomic and geopolitical environment could significantly affect demand for our products and our results of operations. The
L1208@P31: range of events and trends that can impact our business and results of operations includes inflation and interest rates, supply chain disruptions, geopolitical
L1209@P31: pressures, the unknown impact of current and future trade regulations, such as new export controls and tariffs, and geopolitical turmoil, such as any
L1210@P31: changes in PRC-Taiwan relations, the war in Ukraine, and conflicts in the Middle East, including Iran, and fluctuation in foreign exchange rates. For
L1211@P31: example, geopolitical disruption could lead to further market volatility and exacerbate current supply chain constraints, including with respect to certain
L1212@P31: materials and metals that are essential in semiconductor manufacturing. The continuing evolution of global trade policies, and uncertainty in trade relations
L1213@P31: between the U.S. and the PRC and other major U.S. trade partners, has caused, and could continue to cause, market disruptions and supply chain
L1214@P31: constraints. Given the concentration of

L1216@P32: semiconductor manufacturing in East Asia (particularly in Taiwan), any potential escalation in geopolitical tensions in Asia, particularly with respect to
L1217@P32: Taiwan, could significantly disrupt existing semiconductor chip manufacturing and increase the prospect of increased interruption to the semiconductor
L1218@P32: chip supply across the world. The conflicts in Europe and the Middle East have caused no major interruption to our operations to date.
L1219@P32: Ability to Provide Our Customers with More Value Per Chip
L1220@P32: Complex chips and chiplets are more difficult to develop and take longer to design, which increases the cost of the chip and the risk of delayed or
L1221@P32: missed timelines. We believe our ability to continue to develop more advanced products and offer increasingly comprehensive product packages, including
L1222@P32: providing more complete subsystems, such as Arm's CSS solutions which are pre-integrated and pre-verified configurations of Arm technology, will
L1223@P32: encourage greater use of our products by existing and prospective customers. For example, many licensees have historically combined multiple different
L1224@P32: Arm CPUs in a single chip, Arm CPUs with other Arm IP such as Arm GPUs, or deploy Arm CPU implementations with more than 100 cores. Increasing
L1225@P32: cost and time-to-market pressures mean some customers may be better served by the integration of our IP into a subsystem. For chips where our products
L1226@P32: have provided more value, we will typically receive higher royalty revenue per chip. Accordingly, we believe that our investments in higher performance,
L1227@P32: higher efficiency, and more specialized designs will drive greater demand for our products and higher value for our customers, which is expected to result
L1228@P32: in higher royalty revenue. Our future performance is dependent on our continued ability to provide value to customers, and our ability to drive additional
L1229@P32: value through technological innovation.
L1230@P32: Our Market Share Across End Markets
L1231@P32: Arm CPUs are the world’s most widely licensed and deployed processors. Our products are used in almost all smartphones, the majority of tablets and
L1232@P32: digital TVs, and a significant proportion of all chips with embedded processors, including for both consumer and enterprise applications. news L98: ### NVIDIA Unveils Vera, the CPU for Agents
L99: 
L100: May 31, 2026
L101: 
L102: Download this Press Release PDF Format (opens in new window)
L103: 
L104: 1.8x Faster Than x86 Processors to Drive Diverse Workloads Across Industries, Generating More Data Center Token Revenue
L105: 
L106: News Summary:
L107:   * NVIDIA launches high-performance, energy-efficient NVIDIA Vera CPUs to drive diverse workloads across industries, including agentic AI, reinforcement learning and data processing.
L108:   * Vera serves as the CPU powering standalone Vera servers, NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems and Vera BlueField-4 STX AI storage platforms.
L109:   * Global AI labs planning to adopt Vera to transform their AI factories include Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI, and hyperscalers ByteDance, CoreWeave and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
L110:   * Manufacturers building standalone Vera CPU systems at scale include Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro, along with ASUS, Compal, Foxconn, GIGABYTE, Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Wistron and Wiwynn.
L111: TAIPEI, Taiwan, May 31, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA GTC Taipei -- NVIDIA today announced that the world’s technology leaders are planning to adopt cite27†NVIDIA Vera†www.nvidia.com , the first CPU built for AI agents.
L112: 
L113: Now in full production, NVIDIA Vera is a new class of processor enabling 1.8x faster task completion compared with x86 CPUs to drive diverse workloads across industries — including agentic AI, reinforcement learning and data processing — generating more data center token revenue.
L114: Building on the success of NVIDIA Grace™ CPUs, which have nearly 2.5 million shipments to date, Vera takes CPU performance and energy efficiency to new levels for the most demanding AI workloads in modern data centers — where agents move from answering basic questions to taking actions, running code, using tools and evaluating results.
L115: Customers exploring the Vera CPU include finance leader NYSE, global AI labs Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI, and hyperscalers ByteDance, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Vera is also being integrated into AI infrastructure from world-leading system manufacturers such as Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro, along with Taiwan system builders.
L116: “AI agents will be the largest users of computing,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Vera is the first CPU designed for that future — built to run agentic AI at hyperscale with extraordinary performance, efficiency and programmability.”
L117: “At the NYSE, our focus is to optimize the latency, throughput and reliability of the systems underpinning our unrivaled infrastructure,” said Lynn Martin, president of NYSE Group. “The NYSE processes more than 1.1 trillion messages per day, and in collaboration with Redpanda and HPE, using NVIDIA Vera CPUs, we will be scaling our capacity while further optimizing latency to power a high-performance, resilient and AI-ready market infrastructure.”
L118: Anthropic, the AI innovator behind Claude, is evaluating adding Vera to scale CPU-intensive agentic workloads.
L119: 
L120: “Scaling compute is an important accelerant for the growth of models,” said James Bradbury, head of compute at Anthropic. “We’re excited to see Vera emerge as a promising part of the ecosystem when solving for agentic workloads.”
L121: 
L122: OCI Supercluster powered by NVIDIA Vera represents the next frontier in hyperscale AI supercomputing.
L123: “Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is rapidly scaling AI infrastructure to meet surging demand for training, inference and agentic AI,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, executive vice president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “By deploying NVIDIA Vera CPUs, OCI will support high-throughput reasoning and data processing workloads across next-generation AI environments.”
L124: According to Phoronix, which offers a comprehensive, open source benchmarking suite, NVIDIA Vera cite28†delivered†blogs.nvidia.com the fastest overall performance across agentic workloads including code compilation, Python, Java and database processing. These workloads sit on the critical path of modern AI factories, including for agent tool use and sandbox execution, where faster CPU performance delivers higher agent throughput and interactivity.
L125: A Custom CPU for the Agentic Era
L126: AI factory economics are shifting from cores per dollar to tokens per dollar, requiring CPUs that complete agentic, data-processing and orchestration work faster and more efficiently.
L127: 
L128: Vera is powered by Olympus, a custom NVIDIA CPU core engineered for the CPU work behind that shift, from Python runtimes and sandboxed code execution to orchestration logic and analytics pipelines.
L129: Vera is built to process more instructions, anticipate application behavior and move data across large numbers of concurrent environments, queries and data processing tasks — featuring 88 Olympus cores, Spatial Multithreading and a LPDDR5X memory subsystem that delivers up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth. This helps agents spend less time waiting on CPU-bound steps and lets AI factories keep accelerators moving.
L130: The Vera CPU can also be deployed across the full AI factory — from the standalone CPU infrastructure to tightly coupled accelerated systems. Vera helps AI factories deliver higher end-to-end throughput and faster time to solution for users, improving responsiveness and efficiency across training, inference and agentic execution.
L131: Vera serves as the host CPU for NVIDIA Vera Rubin platforms through second-generation NVIDIA NVLink™-C2C interconnect technology, which provides up to 1.8TB/s of coherent bandwidth between CPU and GPU. It extends NVIDIA Confidential Computing at rack scale, protecting agentic workloads.
L132: 
L133: The cite29†NVIDIA Vera BlueField-4 STX†nvidianews.nvidia.com processor integrates Vera with high-performance networking, storage acceleration and in-silicon security to create secure-by-design AI-native data platforms.
L134: Extensive Ecosystem Support
L135: Vera CPUs are available in dense, liquid-cooled racks for large-scale agentic AI and reinforcement learning environments, as well as flexible two-socket air-cooled systems for enterprise, cloud, data processing and AI factory deployments.
L136: Leading infrastructure providers offering Vera CPU-based systems include Aivres, ASRock Rack, cite30†ASUS†asus.click , Compal, Dell, Foxconn, GIGABYTE, HPE, Hyve Solutions, Inventec, Lenovo, MiTAC Computing, cite31†MSI†www.msi.com , Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, Wistron and Wiwynn. Major original equipment manufacturers — Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro — will be offering Vera in standalone CPU server configurations, the first standard CPU option beyond x86.
L137: Leading cloud service providers planning to deploy Vera CPUs include Akamai, ByteDance, Cloudflare, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Redpanda, Starburst, Together AI and Vultr.
L138: 
L139: Availability
L140: Vera systems will be available from system builders and cloud partners starting this fall.
